column5: Three main sources for African history: written documents, archaeology, oral tradition, backed by linguistics and anthropology, with no fixed order of importance; each is a message with intentions and needs criticism.

Rival griot lineages' versions are a guarantee for critical history: Bambara and Fula griots from opposing camps agree, strengthening the evidence. Gouro exoteric lineage tradition differs from esoteric secret-society tradition. Validity of oral tradition cross-checked at Koumbi Saleh, Lake Kisale, and Shona 16th-century events agreeing with Portuguese writers (Abraham).

Chronology: average reign and generation lengths vary; 'son' is sometimes sociological; a king may have three or four strong names; Bemba chief lists merge with lists of candidates; eclipses can date reigns; Ki-Zerbo warns against 'psychosis of precision' (end of 11th century rather than 1086 for Koumbi Saleh).

African time is causal but reckoned by concrete acts (Burundi milking and herd-letting hours), seniority matters more than absolute dates, tally devices (Dogon notched wood, a gold nugget a year at Bono Mansu, pebbles in Manding) and fixed external events anchor reign counts.
Hunwick (1973) re-read Ibn Battuta and al-Umari place names and questions whether Niani-on-the-Sankarani was the capital of ancient Mali; Ki-Zerbo notes the argument from silence in it.

Unpublished Ottoman correspondence of May 1577 from Sultan Murad III to Mai Idris Aloma and the Bey of Tunis, found in the Istanbul prime ministry archive, sheds new light on Kanem-Borno diplomacy and the Fezzan (Martin 1969).

Bantu linguistics is a learned battle: Guthrie supports autogenesis; Greenberg argues Bantu belongs in a wider genetic family from Wolof to Baka. Distribution of words for sheep follows the forest edge parallel to it in Central Africa and runs in vertical belts further east (Ehret 1968), showing diffusion routes and the forest as a barrier.

Greenberg shows Kanuri contributed cultural and military terms to Hausa, and Bornu dynastic titles (kaygamma, migira) spread into Cameroon and Nigeria, evidence of Bornu influence on the Hausa states.

Place names need endogenous reading: Leo Africanus's Gaoga is not necessarily Gao (Teda and Kanuri point to a kingdom between Wadai, Darfur and Fertit); 'Yemen' in Sudanese dynastic origins may mean the ancient land of Yam rather than Arabia Felix (Mohammadou).
Ibn Khaldun gives Sundjata's successor as Mansa Uli, glossing Uli as Ali; storytellers still say Mansa Uli means the king with a fair skin: oral and written accounts used together.

Marriage and language: a maternal tongue prevails only where women are taken as wives, not slaves or concubines (Nguni groups keeping or losing language through Sotho wives; Fula of Futa Djalon becoming Malinke or Bambara speakers in Ouassoulou).

Correlation (Thompson 1969) between trade routes with royal commodity monopoly and centralised monarchy (Ghana, Mali, Asante, Lunda) versus Nyakyusa and Xhosa, off such routes, that did not reach a monarchical stage.

Oyo's authority from the ebi (extended family) versus Dahomey's authoritarian monarchy adapted to the slave trade (Akinjogbin 1967); Law (1971) explains Oyo's decline by internal tensions among slaves, royal stewards, provincial representatives and the three royal eunuchs, not mainly external pressure.

Niger delta development rested on earlier endogenous north-south and east-west relations as far as Lagos and the Ijebu country, not only the slave and palm-oil trades (Alagoa 1973), backing Pacheco Pereira's Esmeraldo.

The Beni Hilal irruption into North Africa was long and wrongly pictured as a nihilistic devastating invasion; Ki-Zerbo prefers the 'osmotic' model of migration (Mossi horsemen marrying locally), also applied to the Mfecane.

Race and tribe: Hiernaux says the Fulani are a cultural, not a biological group; Hamitic and brown races are rejected as biological units; the volume avoids the word 'tribe' except for North African Khabbylia.
Meroitic script remains undeciphered, which keeps Meroe silent; Unesco held a Cairo symposium on deciphering it in 1974.

Pottery and bone typology of the Nigero-Chadian Sahara links the pre-Islamic Sao of the Chad basin to cultural areas as far as the Nile and Libyan desert; Ennedi gives eight millennia of pictorial and ceramic styles checked by excavation, carbon dating, flora and fauna and oral tradition.

Unesco founded the Ahmed Baba centre at Timbuktu to collect manuscripts, and manuscripts concerning black Africa remain uninventoried in Moroccan, Algerian and European libraries and in Niger bend private libraries.

Ki-Zerbo says the slave trade, from the 15th to the 20th century, was a severe demographic drain that deprived Africa of stability; this is an assertion of the volume's editor, not measured in the chapter.

Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) is the earliest surviving written history of tropical Africa in the modern sense: his cyclical model of nomad conquest and decay over about three generations, his rule that scraps of information have unequal weight, and a chapter on Mali partly based on the oral tradition then current (de Slane, Histoire des Berberes vol. 2, pp. 105-16), so still an essential base.

Timbuktu's Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash (essentially 17th century) give detailed recent history plus critical accounts of the oral traditions about Ghana and Mali; the Kano Chronicle and Kilwa Chronicle are little more than written recordings of oral tradition; a Kilwa version was used by De Barros in the 16th century, but the Kano Chronicle is not known in writing before about the 19th century.

Kilwa Chronicle: a version was used by the Portuguese historian De Barros in the sixteenth century (translation in Freeman-Grenville 1962, pp. 34-49); the Kano Chronicle has no evidence of written form before about the nineteenth century (Palmer 1928).

The Gonja Chronicle (Kitab al-Ghunja) in Arabic dates from the 18th century in what is now Ghana, and Wilks and others found hundreds of examples of Arabic literacy there; historical writing in Hausa and Swahili using Arabic script did not develop until the 19th century.

Ethiopia has a continuous written tradition in Ge'ez then Amharic for about two millennia, producing historical writing by the 14th century, for example the Chronicles of the Wars of Amda Sion; Periplus c. 100 of our era, Ptolemy c. 150 (surviving version perhaps c. 400) and Cosmas Indicopleustes (647) remain major sources for early East Africa; European missionaries Pero Paez (d. 1622), Almeida (1569-1646) and Job Ludolf (1624-1704) wrote on Ethiopia.

Classical and Arabic authors (Herodotus, Manetho, Pliny, Strabo; al-Masudi c. 950, al-Bakri 1029-94, al-Idrisi 1154, Yaqut c. 1200, Abu al-Fida 1273-1331, al-Umari 1301-49, Ibn Battuta 1304-69, Leo Africanus c. 1494-1552) describe Africa as known to them rather than analysing change; the authority of their information is often unclear; Leo Africanus's information may not all be first-hand; 'history' in his title means natural history.

European sources: Guinea coast from Cadamosto about 1460 to Barbot and Bosman (18th c.), Dapper 1668 as compiler; Lower Zaire and Angola in Pigafetta and Lopez 1591, Cavazzi 1687, Cadornega's 1681 History of the Angolan Wars; traders only described Guinea society while missionaries and pressure on Kongo society produced more history.

Late 18th-century histories of Dahomey (Norris 1789, Dalzel 1793) and Benezet's Guinea (1772) were published as ammunition in the debate over abolishing the slave trade; Dalzel's editor felt he had to justify a history of Dahomey.

Hegel said Africa is not a historical continent; Trevor-Roper in 1963 said there is no African history, only European history in Africa; Newton in 1923 said history begins with writing; Burton's 1864 digression on the Negro's place in nature; Cambridge History of the British Empire gave Africa little, so colonial history differs from African history.

Seligman, Races of Africa (1930) wrote that African civilizations are those of the Hamites; Greenberg (1963) showed Hamitic is at best a linguistic category and Afro-Asiatic replaced it (Hausa Hamitic-speaking farmers ruled by Fulani who speak a Niger-Congo language). Delafosse's 'Judaeo-Syrian' migration founding Ghana; Frobenius the most productive historian of the first four decades of the 20th century, flawed fieldwork and fanciful theories (Atlantis, Etruscans) but data worth rescuing.

Africans wrote histories in Roman script: Reindorf's History of the Gold Coast and Asante (1895), Samuel Johnson's History of the Yorubas (completed 1897, published 1921), Egharevba's Short History of Benin (1934), Kagwa from 1906 in Uganda; Law counts 22 Yoruba local historians published before 1940; Eva Meyerowitz's Akan work sought a Mediterranean ancestry.

Decolonised historiography: Societe Africaine de Culture and Presence Africaine 1947; Ward's History of the Gold Coast 1948; Roland Oliver's lectureship in London 1948; Dike first African history department head at Ibadan 1956; Unesco launched the General History idea in 1966, drafting from 1969; Cairo 1974 symposium on the peopling of Egypt.

African time is often mythical and social: ancestors remain contemporary agents (Mossi ruler told Mansa Musa's envoy he must consult his ancestors before converting), the king embodies social time (Shilluk, Banyoro, Mossi: 'the Mwami is present: the people lives'), and the interregnum is a parenthesis in time; Kikuyu iron origin myth; Songhay double (bya) and ancestor Si.

Authors argue African time is also genuinely historical and dynamic: if people only repeated ancestors Ibn Battuta would have found cave dwellers, not the empire of Mali; leaders are not reduced to one-man history (Sundjata, Osei Tutu and Anokye, Shaka) because dynamic groups and companions including griots are remembered; griots under official control had near-monopoly of official truth but were not monolithic.

Shaka forged the Zulu nation in combat; oral and written evidence about his activity may have been reproduced many times in African history; at the end of his career Shaka experienced the option of secession and flight that people had against dictatorship (authors' view of a democratic conception of history).

Role of Osei Tutu and Anokye in founding the Asante nation corresponds to the Asante's own conception to the present day; Dahomey Amazons were the spearhead of the royal army against Oyo and the colonial invaders at the Battle of Cana (1892).

Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash praise al-Hajj Askiya Muhammad's virtues and relate them to his good fortune, though both had material interests; Muhammad Bello urged Yacuba Baoutchi to study Songhai: Askiya Muhammad maintained and increased Sonni Ali's legacy through justice, and his sons' departure from the justice of Islam led to disintegration; Bello's account of Uthman dan Fodio's government as justice, and the slaying of Yunfa of Gobir.
Women in history: Amina of Zaria is said to have conquered many Hausa towns in the 15th century; Sonianke kassey priestess at Wanzarba; Songhay matrilineal succession 'through the milk'.
Lueji (Swana Mulunda, Mother of the Lunda People) was in turn daughter, sister, wife and mother of a king; presented as an example of women's authority in Lunda tradition.

Age-group and generation systems can trace history back to the 18th century (Alladians of Moosou organised into five generations each reigning nine years); stateless societies' secret groups (lo of Senufo, poro of Upper Guinea) held moral authority and could usurp power; age counted by rainy seasons.

column5: Wilks, reviewing Henige's The Chronology of Oral Tradition: Quest for a Chimera, shows the Akan had a calendar with a seven-day week, six-week month and nine-month year, realigned on the sun, so that a date such as the eighteenth day of the fourth month of Osei Bonsu's reign could be given; this answers sceptics who say oral traditions cannot be dated.

column5: Akan calendar of seven-day week, six-week month and nine-month year allowed dating within a reign (Wilks 1975), still used in the 18th and 19th centuries.

Civilization was long defined by literacy, yet most of Africa had scribes: Ge'ez in Ethiopia, Arabic from the north coast, Sahara, northern Sudan fringe from Senegal to the Red Sea and east coast cities to the Mozambique Channel, Dyula traders carrying Arabic into the forest, and European languages written along western coasts; Western authorities drew the line at the desert edge, separating North African history.

Early recovery of African history argued on opponents' terms by pointing to kingdoms and empires; Curtin calls this weak, since empires are often cruel and not necessarily progress, and Africa's great achievement in law and politics was probably the stateless society based on co-operation, plus states that preserved local autonomy.

Colonial archives reflect foreign officials' bias, so analytical history needs field history from oral interviews; oral tradition work came in two clusters (1890-1914 scholar-administrators, and the last fifteen years); Murdock 1959 called indigenous oral traditions 'completely undependable'; Vansina's Oral Tradition (1961) showed the critical controls needed; Dakar 1961 and Dar es Salaam 1965 seminars stressed oral tradition, linguistics and archaeology.

The 'anthropological present': functionalist anthropologists (Malinowski) fixed a pre-conquest static model by subtracting external influences, sought out simple isolated societies, left gaps on large complex African societies, and wrongly assumed change came only from outside; historians showed precolonial institutions, religions and economies changed as rapidly as societies between the agricultural and industrial revolutions.

No precolonial African community was self-sufficient with no trade: many Saharan-fringe pastoralists earned half or more of their annual calorie intake by exchanging animal products for cereals, and farmers sold surpluses to buy salt, cattle, shea butter, kola nuts or dates; Curtin rejects Myint's 'vent-for-surplus' picture of subsistence economies.

Shaykh Musa Kamara of Senegal wrote Zuhur ul-Basatin fi Tarikh is-Sawadin, not yet published in full and only recently used; before 1950 African clergy such as Reindorf and Johnson wrote history in international languages.

Combined sources are the method: no 'auxiliary sciences'; example Mdaga mound in Chad, occupied almost 2500 years from the 5th century before our era to the mid 19th century, restored the legendary Sao to authenticated history only by joining oral tradition, rare Arabic manuscripts, excavation and carbon-14 dating.

Pollen analysis (palynology) can show whether farming was practised on a site; staple domesticates cited as sorghum (domesticated in savanna from Lake Chad to the Ethiopia-Sudan border), millet, African rice, Voandzeia, oil palm, finger millet, gumbo, African yam; archaeology and palaeobotany, not oral tradition, answer questions on early agriculture.

Manioc reached the Kingdom of Kongo via the Atlantic coast only after the sixteenth century: Pigafetta and Lopez (1591) list for the Mbanza Kongo plateau only eleusine (luko), a sorghum (masa ma Kongo), maize (masango), rice (loso), banana (dikondo) and oil palm; American maize is fed to pigs and rice little valued.
African crops travelled out: millet and finger millet attested archaeologically in India about 1000 before our era; sorghum later, as Sanskrit has no word for it.

Horse reached Egypt towards the end of the Hyksos invasion, around 1600 before our era; Libyans about the 13th century before our era; Nubians early in the first millennium before our era; rest of Africa made little use before the Arab conquests; two saddled horses among the emblems of the king of Mali (Ibn Battuta). Camel: Chad Sahara rock painting of the 3rd century before our era; Cambyses introduced it to Egypt in 525 before our era; carried to the Maghrib by Roman troops of Syrian origin; Berbers used it to settle beyond the limes, pushing sedentary blacks of oases south or into slavery.

Egyptian scripts: hieroglyphic, hieratic (about third dynasty), demotic (about 25th dynasty), latest hieroglyphic text dated 394 of our era, Demotic and Meroitic share an origin in graphemes; Meroitic not deciphered; letter of Pepi II (about 2370 before our era) to Herkhuf on a southern expedition that brought back a pygmy; Tale of the Castaway (twelfth dynasty, 20th century before our era) on Red Sea navigation; Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt in her ninth year (reign 1504-1483 before our era) shown at Deir el-Bahri.

Quoting the Cairo 1974 symposium report, Obenga says Egyptian is not a Semitic language and urges dropping 'Hamito-Semitic' or 'Afro-Asiatic' labels, seeking comparison with black African languages; this conflicts with the standard Afro-Asiatic classification used elsewhere in the course and in Fage (ch. 1) and Greenberg.

Obenga links African scripts to Egyptian hieroglyphs (Gicandi of the Kikuyu, Nsibidi of the Efik, Mende, Loma, Vai, Bamum, Dogon-Bambara-Bozo signs) and says Egyptian writing had 'unbroken revivals' between the 17th and 19th centuries, but concedes many of these systems are recent and do not illuminate early periods; the claim of causal connection rests on resemblance, not documented transmission.

Reconstructed 'common Bantu' or proto-Bantu denotes a system of correlations between known languages, not an ancient language restored; common language does not imply racial identity; Niger-Congo links West Atlantic, Mande, Gur, Kwa, Benue-Congo, Adamawa-Eastern and Bantu peoples; Mbochi history reconstructed only through oral tradition; Loango royal burials at Lubu and Lwandjili explained by Vili tradition of a quarrel between the Maloango court and Lwandjili where written records of 1753 and 1776 are silent.

Excavations at Tegdaoust (Aoudaghost) from 1960 by Devisse and D. and S. Robert combined local tradition, medieval Arab chronicles and archaeology to recover the 7th to 13th centuries of the Ghana kingdom area.

Griots usually give no chronological framework and treat each moment as having its own meaning (Obenga's 'absolute history' or structural history); cycles, periods, eras, ages and series are virtually absent from their vocabulary.

Kingdom of Kongo (nsi a Kongo, the country of the Kongo) is described as an ethnic region and one huge chiefdom where the king (mfumu) is eldest son and maternal uncle of every matrilineal clan (makanda) recognising founder-ancestors, ntinu as supreme chief; not a state ruled by a king in the Western sense.

Kingdom of Danxome (Dahomey) is closer to absolute monarchy: heartland, central authority of king, ministers and their delegates (Glele), king as dokunno owner of wealth with power of life and death over anato (men of the people), glesi farm workers on royal estates; chiefs act in his name; annexed Fon, Mahi, Alada, Savi, Juda; consent via palaver and chiefdoms.

The word feudalism has legalistic (fief, loyalty, homage) and Marxist (serfs tied to land, mode of production) senses; Obenga says comparative sociology is lacking; the Bariba of Benin are a working hypothesis of African 'feudalism'; so-called feudal tendencies may rest on social and economic relationships, not fiefs.

Written sources before the 15th century split by period (antiquity to 622; first Islamic age to 1050; second Islamic age 1050-1450), region (five zones, not 'two Africas') and type (narrative vs archival); pyramid of languages: Arabic, Greek, Latin, Egyptian, Coptic, Hebrew, Aramaic, Ethiopic, Italian, Persian, Chinese; narrative sources dominate until the 12th century, archival from the 12th and almost none for black Africa; Africa's New Kingdom papyri are the oldest archives in the world (twenty centuries before the Ravenna papyri).

Central and southern Africa have a void in written sources before the 15th century, but the historian must not make value judgements from documents or neglect what they offer; Arabic sources emphasising the Sudan may suggest it was the only centre of organised states; sources are a framework of external cultures but can be read in an African context with care about ideological presuppositions.

Arabic geographers: Kubbel and Matveiev list 40 authors on black Africa to the 12th century, 21 of them geographers; critical questions to ask: how much is reality and how much hackneyed Adab themes, how much Greek, Iranian or Arabic heritage, how much compilation or observation; only a handful give original information (Ibn Khurdadhbah, Ya'qubi d. 897, Mas'udi, Ibn Hawqal fl. 977); Djait rejects both Islamophobic and introverted Africanist rejection of these sources.

Ya'qubi mentions the Zaghawa of Kanem and the great kingdom of Ghana and its gold; Ibn Hawqal (fl. 977) visited Nubia and possibly the western Sudan and is valuable on Maghrib-Sudan trade; Ibn al-Faqih has something on Ghana and Kuku; Buzurg ibn Shahriyar on the east coast and Zanj.

Ibadite chronicle of Ibn al-Saghir on Rustamid Tahert shows trade links between Tahert and Gao by the end of the 8th century; Djait warns that Lewicki's deductions from such allusive hagiographical sources are too bold; sources must be cross-checked.

Almoravid and Almohad official letters have been published (Laroui: one can now see Almohadism from inside); Geniza documents are in Arabic in Hebrew script and undated; Italian archives of Venice, Genoa, Pisa and Barcelona hold treaties, contracts and letters for Egypt and the Maghrib.

Al-Bakri (fl. 1068) did not travel in the Maghrib or Sudan but used the lost notes of al-Warraq and first-hand reports from merchants and travellers; al-Idrisi's Book of Roger (1154) borrows from predecessors; Ibn Said (before 1286) draws on a 12th-century traveller Ibn Fatima for the Sudan; al-Umari's Masalik al-Absar is the main source for Mali's organisation and Egypt links and for the Muslim states of 14th-century Ethiopia.

Djait's table dates Almoravid conquest of Ghana to 1076 and Mansa Musa to 1312-35, and Mali collapse before Songhai's emergence; elsewhere in vol. I Hama and Ki-Zerbo give Mansa Musa 1312-32; the Almoravid conquest of Ghana is disputed in vols III and IV.
