column5: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea assigned to c. 230 of our era by Djait (once assigned to the 1st century; Fage gives c. 100); Cosmas Indicopleustes c. 535 (Fage gives 647); Ptolemy's Geography c. 140 (Fage c. 150); the Ethiopic oldest writing 13th century (Djait) while Fage says Ge'ez histories by the 14th century.

Egyptian hieratic papyri and ostraca of the Ramessid period (1314-1085 before our era) include civil service, legal, accounting, letters and stories; legal papyri (Abbott, Amherst, Mayer, Turin) underlie knowledge of Rameses IX to XI; nothing written is known of Nubia and Punt without new discoveries; the Book of Kings (before 586, reworked in Exile) gives the 22nd dynasty about 950 before our era; the Elephantine papyri are the fifth-century source and the Demotic Chronicle for the fourth and third; Pliny's Natural History gives trade routes of Ethiopia.

North African antiquity: Carthage's own history survives almost wholly in Greek and Latin writers (Polybius 200-120 chief source, seems present at the siege of Carthage 146 before our era; Sallust on Jugurtha; Procopius De Bello Vandalico for Vandal/Byzantine Africa; Victor Vitensis and Corippus penetrate the interior); Donatism known mainly through Augustine, so caution; Periplus of Hanno is spurious, composite, not earlier than 1st century before our era.

Roman expeditions beyond the limes (Balbus 19 before our era, Flaccus 70, Maternus 86) informed Ptolemy's map of Inner Libya; ancients probably did not go beyond Cape Juby, so classical writings give an image of Africa and not data on western black Africa; Herodotus reports Carthaginian silent trade in southern Morocco.

First Arabic chronicle of the Maghrib: Khalifa b. Khayyat (d. 240 AH), Ibn Abd al-Hakam's Futuh Misr wa l-Maghrib (a collection of legal traditions, caution advised, includes the Baqt treaty with Nubia); Kindi's Wulat Misr (d. 961) for the 8th-century Maghrib; Umar b. Shabba records a revolt of the Sudan at Medina in 145 AH/762 of our era.

Chinese sources are mostly 15th century and concern the East African coast; one text is from the second half of the 11th century; Masudi's Fields of Gold (965) is dense with information on the Zanj and east coast; Buzurg ibn Shahriyar on the east coast.

Mahrams (letters patent) issued by the kings of Bornu, those of Umm Jilmi and the Masbarma family, probably date from the late 11th century (Mauny 1961), the oldest archival documents from black Africa.

After 1500 sources diversify: archival material (letters, reports, deeds) appears; external Arabic sources decline and Africans south of the Sahara write in Arabic from the early 16th century, later in African languages in Arabic script (Kiswahili, Hausa, Fulfulde, Kanembu, Dyula, Malagasy), later in Latin; European narratives give a chronological framework (one traveller's date can anchor a chronology) and good economic detail but misread inner social structure; later is not automatically more objective (Burton and Stanley were prisoners of racial theory as the Portuguese were of religion); 19th-century explorers were more interested in waterways than in ways of life (Mazrui).

Primary documents: Arabic letters from the Ottoman Sultan to Mai Idris of Bornu 1578 and from Morocco to the Askiya and Kanta of Kebbi; the Asantehene's Arabic chancery at Kumasi with letters in Copenhagen; a 1776 Arabic treaty between the slave trader Morice and the sultan of Kilwa; thousands of 19th-century Arabic documents of Sokoto, Macina, Bornu, al-Hajj Umar, Samory and others; Unesco and International Council on Archives Guides to Sources (Germany 1970, Spain 1971, France, Italy, Scandinavia, Netherlands); archives made in Africa hold mostly records from the 1880s.

Vai script invented about 1833 by Momolu Duwalu Bukele and used by nearly all Vai by 1900 for letters, accounts and customary laws, adapted by Mende, Loma, Kpelle and Bassa; Bamum script by Sultan Njoya (reformed four times) with a book on Bamum history and customs; Nsibidi inscriptions in the Cross River valley used in secret societies.

Koelle Polyglotta Africana (1854) has vocabularies of about 160 languages; Kikongo grammar by Brusciotto (1659) and dictionary by De Gheel (d. 1652) allow diachronic study of social and cultural vocabulary.

Shungwaya, origin of many eastern Bantu migration traditions, is not a known place today but appears on Van Linschoten's 1596 and Blaeu's 1662 maps as a town and later an area near the coast (Randles 1958).

Ethiopia has royal chronicles since the 13th century; Ahmad Gran's invasion in the first half of the 16th century is covered by the Royal Chronicle of Lebna Dengel, by Arab-Faqih's chronicle written in 1543 and by Portuguese eyewitness Castanhoso; Bahrey's History of the Galla (1593); a Yemeni ambassador's account of a 1647 mission to Fasiladas, for whom no Ethiopian chronicle survives; Rubenson's analysis of the Amharic text of the Wichale treaty (1889).

Eastern Sudan: Funj Chronicle written down in the closing years of the Funj sultanate, early 19th century, from oral tradition; Wad Dayfallah's Tabaqat dictionary for the Funj kingdom; David Reubeni visited in 1523; Mahdiyya records number about 80 000 Arabic documents in Khartoum.

Hrbek says the earliest extant Sudanic chronicles date from the early sixteenth century yet describes Tarikh al-Fattash (three generations of the Kati family of Jenne, to the Moroccan conquest of 1591) and Tarikh al-Sudan (al-Sadi of Timbuktu, to 1655); Fage in chapter 1 says both were essentially composed in the seventeenth century; Ahmad Baba (d. 1627) compiled a biographical dictionary; Tadhkirat al-nisyan covers the Moroccan pashas of Timbuktu 1591-1751; Tarikh Say by Ibn Adwar, said to be 1410, looks like a later version of oral tradition.

column4: Hrbek, ch. 6, p. 135 and Ki-Zerbo, introduction p. 6
column5: Hrbek dates the Ottoman Sultan's letter to Mai Idris of Bornu as 1578, while Ki-Zerbo's introduction gives May 1577 for a letter from Murad III to Mai Idris Aloma and the Bey of Tunis.

Chronicle writing spread from Timbuktu and Jenne: Kitab al-Ghunja written after 1752; Futa Jallon and Futa Toro chronicles (Sire-Abbas Soh); Imam Ibn Fartuwa's late 16th-century account of Mai Idris and his wars; Bornu mahrams as deeds of privilege; little pre-jihad Hausa material survives; chronicles of Kano, Katsina and Abuja are late 19th-century but partly derived from earlier documents; al-Hajj Umar Tall's Rimah Hizb al-Rahim; the unpublished Zuhur al-Basatin on Futa Toro by Shaykh Musa Kamara.

Moroccan historians: al-Ufrani (d. c. 1738) covered 1511-1670; al-Zayyani (d. 1833) described 1631-1812; al-Nasiri (d. 1897); Moroccan historians also recorded the Songhay fall and later Niger valley history; Mauritanian chronicles of Nema, Walata and Shinqit cover adjoining Sudan.

Kilwa Chronicle composed about 1530, in two versions (one transmitted by De Barros, another copied in Zanzibar in 1877); most coastal chronicles are recent recorded oral tradition; over 30 000 pages of Swahili and Arabic manuscripts found since 1965; Kitab al-Zanj on southern Somalia and northern Kenya (Cerulli 1957); al-Inkishafi poem on Pate composed in the second decade of the 19th century.

Ahmad ibn Majid (early 16th century), pilot who led Vasco da Gama from Malindi to India, wrote nautical works with strong opinions on the Portuguese; Chronicle of the Fortress of Aden by Abu Makhrama (d. 1540); Leo Africanus (al-Hasan al-Wazzan) travelled as a Muslim before conversion and supplied Europe for nearly three centuries with its only real knowledge of the interior, with mistakes.

Portuguese knew the whole coast from the Senegal to Cape Guardafui by the early 16th century and penetrated Kongo, Angola and the Zambezi late in the century; Historical Documents of East and Central Africa (about 20 volumes from 1965) publishes Portuguese documents on South-East Africa; Cuvelier and Jadin edited Vatican documents on old Kongo.

South Africa: no African-written sources before the 19th century; Zulu traditions collected in the 1880s but published later by A. T. Bryant (use with caution); early observers Isaacs and Fynn untrained and inaccurate about non-whites; letters of Moshesh, Dingaan, Cetshwayo, Mzilikazi and Lobengula; Moffat, Casalis, Arbousset and Livingstone describe the interior; Kolb (1705-12) first detailed Cape account; Isidigimi (1870-80) and Imvo Zabantsundu (from 1884) vernacular newspapers.

Early African writers in European languages: Ignatius Sancho (1781), Ottobah Cugoano (1787) and Olaudah Equiano (1789) are polemical but rich in biography; Antera Duke diary of Calabar in pidgin English survives only as extracts for 1785-7; the slave trade period was unfavourable to objective reporting but trade needs required close attention to economic systems.

Antera Duke, leading Calabar trader, kept a diary in pidgin English, original destroyed in Scotland in the Second World War; Reindorf (1895) and Johnson (published 1921) start an unbroken chain of African historians; Dalzel's History of Dahomy proves on close investigation to be an anti-abolitionist pamphlet.

Definition: a tradition is a testimony transmitted verbally from one generation to the next; valid tradition should rest on an eyewitness account; rumour is excluded; origins of traditions are eyewitness testimony, rumour, or new creation; Islamic hadith criticism (isnad chain) used the same credibility tests as modern criticism; a Rwandan informant gave two incompatible traditions on Tutsi and Hutu (fell from heaven versus brothers).

Four forms: formula, poem, epic and narrative (fixed or free wording; set or free form); fixed forms allow archetype reconstruction but are hermetic and need commentary; narratives are freely recast; stock themes (migratory legends such as the chief killed by a mat over a pit of stakes, found from Luba to Fula, Hausa and Mossi) should be explained, not used to reject the whole tradition; aesthetic distortion: the more a recital fits the standard of excellence, the more it is distorted.

Social framework: every tradition has a social surface; official versus private traditions (family histories less distorted by the state but poorly transmitted); varied profiles by society (Gouro secret-society history, Tonga rainmakers' centres, Teke royal tradition only two generations deep); a tradition that contradicts its function is likely true (a people saying it is younger, a chronicle admitting defeat); Goody and Watt's homeostasis and 'structural amnesia' only partial; esoteric and exoteric traditions (Asante royal family knew a secret origin story; Biiru ritual specialists in Rwanda; Ogboni traditions distorted); Dogon Sigi ritual every sixty years; variants count reflects fidelity.

Mental framework: stereotypes of kings (the magician, the just, the warrior) distort attribution of wars; Igala founders hunters versus kings reflecting two historical situations (Boston); McGaffey on four Kongo ideal positions; time units (market weeks, initiations, reigns, generations, a calendar of catastrophes); social memory depth depends on institution (family three generations; clan, age-group, royalty farther; Sudanic traditions of Tekrur, Ghana and Mali go back to the 11th century); Teke telescope everything into odd and even generations; direction axes (Kuba migrate from downstream sacred to upstream profane) make migration narratives cosmology; most West African peoples cite the east as origin; Beidelman and structuralists overdo denial of narrative value, a tradition can be rejected only when symbolic invention is probable and provable.

Chronology: oral chronology is relative and shortens or lengthens; segmentary societies drop 'useless' ancestors so genealogical depth stays constant; king lists omit usurpers and uninitiated kings, merge abdicated and returned reigns, and under indirect rule colonial pressure lengthened dynasties; interlacustrine regularised father-to-son successions; irregularities are a guarantee of authenticity; statistical study gives average dynastic generation 26 to 32 years (reign length too variable); convert by projecting averages from a first written date, precise only for beginnings of sequences or about once a century, and mark calculated dates with a siglum (example 'Kuba kingdom foundation c. 1635'); synchronisms valid only to three units (A=B=C); eclipses give absolute dates.

Evaluation: two independent sources that agree turn probability into near certainty but independence must be proved; contamination from Imbangala, Dyula and Hausa caravans, indirect-rule histories, and written histories by Johnson (Oyo) and Kagwa (Buganda) which influenced later Yoruba and Ganda dynastic lists; iconatrophy: attributing visible ruins to 'first inhabitants' (Tellem, Sirikwa) is not independent; Koumbi Saleh and Lake Kisale confirm oral tradition; an immediate archaeological datum overrides an oral inference; written quantity is often more reliable but oral motives more accurate; compromise between contradictory sources often makes no sense.

Collecting: long residence, language, tones checked by a linguist, all variants, sampling by rules of variant formation; informants contaminated by textbooks, radio, early colonial reports taken over as ancestral truth; plan around a historical problem; publish informants and cite each oral source separately (not 'Tradition has it that'); traditions mostly relate to the 19th century and rarely date before 1700, some scholars say 1800; Cavazzi's 17th-century traditions became usable after fieldwork in 1970; interlacustrine sites show remote first centuries of our era but dates come only from archaeology; Sundjata epic hides remote history; traditions are best for explaining change within a culture, poor for chronology and quantities, and subsidiary to archaeology before the last few centuries.

Relevant to the Zulu and mfecane: oral chronologies rarely date before 1700 and are distorted by regularisation of genealogies and attribution of wars to a stereotype warrior king; the Zulu traditions' later collection means dates for Shaka's reign need written anchors.

Griots are troubadours who perform agreed versions at marriages, deaths and chiefs' feasts; Mossi Bend-naba chief of the drums belongs to the ruling class; Sudanese traditions of Tekrur, Ghana and Mali supported by Arab and Sudanese authors go back to the 11th century; Imbangala, Dyula and Hausa merchants carry fragments of history that local tradition incorporates.

Asante royal family knew a secret origin story while the public knew the official version; Ogboni traditions of the Yoruba country distorted to legitimise a small group's power; Johnson's Oyo history contaminated later Yoruba dynastic lists written to match models.

Interlacustrine regularisation of successions (son following father far above world average) lengthens dynasties; colonial indirect-rule pressure lengthened lists with repeated royal names; Kagwa's Buganda history shaped later Ganda lists; remote interlacustrine sites recalled only as the 'first centuries of our era' by tradition, dated by archaeology; Cavazzi's Upper Kwango traditions summarise changes over perhaps a thousand years before 1500 without dates.

Writing is not inherently more faithful than oral testimony: each is human evidence worth the person; speech in savanna traditions (Bambara Komo, Fulani) is treated as sacred and creative, lying is a ritual interdict for officiants and traditionalists (domas, silatiquis), and the Komo chanter cites his chain of teachers; these ideas come from the savanna zone of former French West Africa, not the forest, and the author says so.

Griot (dieli) is a caste of public entertainers, genealogists and ambassadors with licence to have 'two tongues' and embellish; distinguished from the doma (initiated traditionalist) who is bound by truth; people ask 'a dieli story or a doma story?'; a dieli can become a doma by initiation except in Komo; French took griots for witches by confusing subaa and subaga; nyamakala castes (smith, weaver, woodworker, leather-worker, dieli) rank with smith highest; caste hierarchy in Mande appeared with empires where warriors claimed supremacy; earlier silatiquis, not ardos, governed Fulani communities.

Genealogists travel widely: Molom Gaolo (d. about 1968 at 105) held about forty generations of Fulani genealogy; the Gaolo class equals nyamakala; genealogy serves identity and settles land disputes; in old Mali everyone knew ten or twelve generations of forebears.

Islam did not alter oral transmission but adapted to it: isnad and silsila chains parallel the traditionalist chain; oral Islamic schools taught in Fulfulde (Djelgodji, Barani, Uthman dan Fodio's school); Kunta Arab-Berber family islamised the region before the 11th century; children memorised the Koran in Arabic without understanding it.

Hampate Ba's method for the History of the Fulani Empire of Macina in the Eighteenth Century (with Daget, 1962): over fifteen years, about a thousand informants from Futa Jallon to Kano; compared Macinanke and Tukulor versions and others; kept only statements agreeing across rival traditions; found the thread constant and differences minor; Monteil found stories collected by his father fifty years earlier unchanged; the Thianaba serpent legend led engineer Belime about 1921 to find the former bed of the Niger.

Break in transmission: the 1914 war took young men away before their initiations, colonial schools and acculturation followed; the author sets a ten to fifteen year window to collect the last great repositories; researcher advice 'heart of a dove, skin of a crocodile, stomach of an ostrich'; 'putting in the straw': traditionalists hoodwinked colonial anthropologists unwilling to be initiated.

Baule gold was seen as a divine metal; anyone could extract it but nuggets above a standard weight went back to the god and swelled royal sacred gold that kings could not draw from, handed down intact until the European occupation; Tukulor followers of al-Hajj Umar who came to Macina kept their genealogies in Senegalese Futa.

Smiths: Bambara numu or Fulfulde baylo; three kinds (mining or smelting smith, blacksmith, jeweller attached to a chief); smith ranks highest of the nyamakala, ritual purification before work, only smiths circumcise; iron smelting connected with sacred forge Fan; Hampate Ba says the high-furnace operator knows mineralogy and can find gold by plants.

Archaeometry must be one criterion alongside stratigraphy, philology and style; identification must rest on chemical or X-ray examination, not visual appearance: copper is confused with bronze and bronze with brass, which was first made about the middle of the first century before our era while bronze was used some twenty centuries earlier.

Radiocarbon dates match Egyptian historical chronology back to about 1800 before our era (Senusret III) using a half-life of 5730; earlier samples diverge and need the Stuiver-Suess correction, after which dates agree within 50 to 100 years; example: reeds from the mastaba of Qaa' dated 2450 plus or minus 65 uncorrected, 2928 plus or minus 65 corrected, historical 2900 before our era; radiocarbon reaches only about 70 000 years; wood or charcoal dates the cutting of the tree, not its use.

Thermoluminescence dates the firing of pottery to an accuracy of about plus or minus 10 per cent, hoped no better than 5 per cent, but suits sites with pottery and few organic remains; archaeomagnetic dating not yet tried in Africa in 1981; Akori dichroic glass beads fall into two chemical groups, group A found in older inland West African sites (430 to 1290 of our era) and group B in younger contexts; southern African rock paintings dated by amino acids to 1200-1800 years for the White Lady.

Trace elements show trade: Egyptian predynastic obsidian is from Ethiopia, implying early trade; nickel content distinguishes meteoric from smelted iron (Tutankhamun's dagger is meteoric); prospecting by air photography, phosphate soil analysis, pollen analysis (needs a radiocarbon scale for dating), resistivity and magnetic surveying to find buried furnaces and kilns.

Iron objects from Niani (Guinea) dated about the 13th to 15th centuries of our era contain copper, phosphorus, nickel, tungsten, titanium and molybdenum as impurities probably from the ores (Muzur and Nosek 1974).
Spectrographic analysis shows the naturalistic Ife 'bronzes' of Nigeria are made of brass, not bronze (Willett 1964).

Linguistic classification comes in genetic, typological and geographical kinds; valid comparison must use forms from the languages' original heritage, not borrowings (some Swahili varieties have over 60 per cent Arabic loans yet Swahili is Bantu); reconstruction by sound shifts gives proto-languages, but shared vocabulary percentages can mislead (Sapir's West Atlantic figures: Baga, Koba and Temne 79 per cent, Serer and Fulani 37 per cent, Temne and Serer 5 per cent).

Glottochronology: Swadesh retention rate of 81 plus or minus 2 to 85 plus or minus 0.4 per cent per 1000 years, with t = log c over 2 log r; Diagne says findings fall short because borrowing and overlapping cannot be separated from normal change; Delafosse's eleventh-century Arabic word lists show Sudanese basic vocabulary almost unchanged over a thousand years.

African language classification is contested and premature: 1300 to 1500 systems of speech; Greenberg's Afro-Asiatic (with a separate Chadic branch) disputed by Polotsky; Cushitic classified three different ways by Greenberg, Tucker and Bryan, and Dolgopolskij (ten subgroups versus three to five); West Atlantic group questioned by Wilson, Dalby and Sapir (5-10 per cent shared vocabulary); Cairo 1974 report that Egyptian cannot be explained as Semitic; classifications of Chadic and Sara may link with Serer, Fulfulde and Wolof.

Ideological distortion: Meinhof wrote that Hamitic peoples constantly subjugated black peoples; Greenberg showed Hausa farmers were conquered by cattle-owning Fulani who speak a Niger-Congo language, so the Hamite-cattle-conquest equation fails; Fulfulde resembles Serer more than any other language yet some scholars sought a white origin for Fulani; Diagne's Wolof and Serer closer to Bantu than to Mande claim is his own view; the term Hamitic can only be used with express qualification.

Methods beyond comparison: onomastics (toponyms with dugu for Mande, saare for Fulani, ker for Wolof, daaru for Arabo-Berbers; Tukulor names show a mixed community of Fulani, Mande, Serer, Lebu-Wolof and Berber); semantic anthropology reads culture from vocabulary; typological cultural diffusion studies (Frobenius, Westermann, Baumann) have overreached by inferring linguistic relationship from cultural features.

Writing in Africa: Diagne argues for a continuous African graphic tradition from the Palette of Narmer to the Recade of Glele, comparing Dahomey recades (Dakodonu, 1625-50; Gezo) with Egyptian picto-phonograms; Vai writing known in Europe 1834 and Koelle 1849; Tafineq of the Tuareg said to have developed under Punic influence; Nubian writing formed in the tenth century through Coptic; Amharic alphabet from Sabean; Meroitic derived from Egyptian or sharing an origin; Cavazzi (1687) and a 1896 Tete inscription cited; the claims of continuity rest on resemblance.

column4: Ki-Zerbo editorial note on races, pp. 261-269
column5: Editorial note on race: morphological and blood-group approaches, more variation within groups than between (Lewontin: over 85 per cent within nations, 7 per cent between nations of one race, 7 per cent between races); Unesco declaration that race is a social myth; Nei and Roychoudhury gene-based divergence estimates (Negroid about 120 000 years, Mongoloid and Caucasoid 55 000 years) are cited; Jacquard's study of 27 populations; Hiernaux on genetic unity of sub-Saharan peoples; Ki-Zerbo stresses history of Africa is not a history of races.

Dahomey recades: royal message axes; Recade of Dakodonu (1625-50, described by Le Herisse) reads as picto-phonograms giving the king's name; Recade of Gezo shows the king as a buffalo; Diagne compares them to the Palette of Narmer, a comparison that rests on likeness of method and not on shown contact.
Berber script Tafineq used by the Tuareg is said to have developed under Punic influence through contact with Carthage.

Nubian writing system formed in the tenth century through contact with Coptic, itself from Greek; Amharic and Tigrinya alphabet derives from Sabean writing of southern Arabia; Meroitic is a continuation of or shares origin with Egyptian writing.

Nineteenth-century German school: Hegel's non-historical Africa, Stuhlmann's waves of Asian immigrants (Pygmies and San, then Negroes, proto-Hamites making Bantu, fair-skinned Hamites, Semites), and Meinhof's linguistic Hamitic theory ranking click, isolating, agglutinative and inflected languages; the theories collapsed with the 1924 Australopithecine find and later palaeoanthropology showing the sequence of human evolution in Africa.

Early Holocene evidence: pottery in Tassili n'Ajjer and Tadrart Acacus from 8000 before our era, a skeleton in skin clothing dated 9000 before our era; wild-cereal gathering in Lower Nubia (Ballana 12050 plus or minus 280, Tuskha 12550 plus or minus 490 before present-era dates), argued to be 4000 years earlier than in the Near East; stock-raising and rudimentary agriculture across Indus to Atlantic before the Fertile Crescent, so the Fertile Crescent is a terminal development.

Language changes faster than physical type (African Americans, Siddi in India, Arabised Maghrib); the early Sahara was inhabited mainly by a black population per rock paintings with Afro-Mediterranean groups also present; as the Sahara dried, peoples retreated to the Nile, lower Senegal, middle Niger and Lake Chad basins where Ethiopoid, Afro-Mediterranean and Sudanic groups mingled; the author warns that lowland-forest and savanna stereotypes are partial.

Pygmies: earliest mention is the letter of Pepi II to Herkhuf about a dwarf called Deng (and an earlier one under Isesi), doko dwarfs in southern Ethiopia, Mongo epic Nsong-a-Lianja says Pygmies were driven into Ituri and Uele forests by Bantu; San and Khoi-Khoi are not a single Khoisan group (differences in stature, pronouns, economy), San once ranged to Kenya (toponyms, rock painting of tall dark warriors with shields), Hadzapi and Sandawe as relics; the kwe ring stones do not prove San settlement since Galla use them; palaeo-African label proposed for San, Kwadi and Hadza.

Olderogge criticises Greenberg's mass-comparison method (sixteen families in 1954, twelve, then four in 1963) as hasty, proposes Zindj for the Niger-Kordofanian and Nilo-Saharan complex (Gregersen 1972 Congo-Saharan), and says Bantu is the only well-established unit; Bantu genesis theories: north from Cameroon or Chad skirting the forest (Greenberg-type), directly through the forest (Johnston), or Guthrie's core among Luba and Bemba.

Bantu is only a linguistic label: Bantu-speakers differ in physique, matrilineal or patrilineal descent, masks and secret societies, and the Portuguese found Bubi (Bantu) speakers on Fernando Po ignorant of iron, so iron cannot be tied to Bantu speech; Olderogge notes copper deposits and workings in Guthrie's nuclear Bantu area and suggests mode of production often drove language expansion; the Sahara's drying pushed Sudanic cattle breeders and hunters out to moister areas and displaced indigenous groups south.

On Bantu origins for the lakes and Kongo lessons: Greenberg-type northern route round the forest, Johnston's direct route through the Zairean forest, and Guthrie's Luba-Bemba core are three named positions; Fernando Po Bubi had no iron, so Bantu speech does not prove iron; copper in the Guthrie core area may have driven expansion.

Genetic classification groups languages by descent from a common ancestor (as Indo-European branches), so reflects ethnic differentiation and supports inferences on non-linguistic cultural history; resemblances in both sound and meaning (roots and grammatical formants) count as evidence, typological features such as tone or sex gender do not.

History of classification: seventeenth-century notes (Malagasy like Malay; Mozambique and Angola languages similar; Ludolf on Ge'ez); Koelle's Polyglotta Africana from Freetown; Bleek named Bantu in 1851; Lepsius (noun class, gender languages 'depositories of civilisation') and Muller (hair type) dominate 1860 to 1910; Westermann 1911 Sudanic and Meinhof 1912 Hamitic (adding Fulani, Masai and Khoi-Khoi on gender) gave a fivefold scheme; Westermann's 1927 work already showed West Sudanic resemblance to Bantu; Delafosse limited Hamitic to Berber, Egyptian and Cushitic.

Greenberg's 1949-50 classification: four families (Niger-Congo later Niger-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic with five branches Berber, Egyptian, Semitic, Cushitic, Chadic, Nilo-Saharan, Khoisan), Hausa the only Meinhof extension kept (in Chadic), Khoi-Khoi classed as San, Hamitic dropped as arbitrary; Table 12.1 shows his own revisions (sixteen families in 1949-50, twelve in 1954, four in 1963); Fleming proposes Omotic as a sixth Afro-Asiatic branch.

A footnote added at the request of a Committee member says Berber is a Semitic language, one of the oldest of the family, that classing it Hamito-Semitic reflects colonial French Berber scholarship (El Fasi 1971), and that it is neither Hamito-Semitic nor Afro-Asiatic; footnote 27 records that African scholars at the Cairo symposium faulted Greenberg for overlooking phonetic rules and argued Egyptian is genetically related to modern African languages, and Olderogge in ch. 11 disputes the Khoisan family.

Bantu origin: Guthrie held Bantu genetically independent with a nuclear area in southern Shaba and resemblances in other Niger-Congo languages from Bantu influence; Greenberg places Bantu as a sub-group of Benue-Congo within Niger-Congo with origin in the middle Benue valley (Nigeria) because the closest Bantoid languages are spoken there; Mande lacks noun classes so Mukarovsky would put it in Nilo-Saharan (Wemers disagrees); Fula now agreed to be West Atlantic.

Nilo-Saharan includes Songhay, Saharan (Kanuri-Kanembu, Teda-Daza, Zaghawa), Maba, Fur, Chari-Nile (Eastern Sudanic with Nubian and Nilotic, Central Sudanic); Meroitic extinct about the fourth century of our era, known from Aswan to Khartoum, little lexicon known because there are no bilingual inscriptions; Trigger suggests an Eastern Sudanic Nilo-Saharan link with Nubian; Merina is Austronesian, closest to Maanyan of Borneo.

Dalby: the family-tree model oversimplifies; about 120 complex and simple units, over 100 in a sub-Saharan Fragmentation Belt about 5600 km long and 1100 km wide (Senegal to the Ethiopian and East African highlands); about 1650 languages in Africa (1250 to 2050 depending on counting), about 1100 in the belt; two 'areas of wider affinity' (Northern Afro-Asiatic, Southern Niger-Congo) hold over 80 per cent of languages; intermediate groupings such as Benue-Congo, Kwa, Gur, West Atlantic, Cushitic and Chadic are not demonstrated (Stewart/Williamson found no valid shared innovations for Benue-Congo); historians should treat Greenberg's classification with reservation.

The committee note says Berber is Semitic, not Hamito-Semitic or Afro-Asiatic, and that North African linguists criticise colonial French Berber scholarship (El Fasi 1971): a position that conflicts with Greenberg's text placing Berber as one of five Afro-Asiatic branches.

Egyptian documented in hieroglyphs, hieratic, demotic and Coptic (Greek alphabet), extinct as spoken language probably in the seventeenth century; Ethiopian Semitic divides into northern (Tigrinya, Tigre, Ge'ez) and southern (Amharic, Gurage, Argobba, Gafat, Harari); Agau (Central Cushitic) was spoken by the Falasha; Beja is Northern Cushitic; Meroitic's unread status and Trigger's Nubian link.

Songhay is placed in Nilo-Saharan as a western outlier; Kanuri-Kanembu, Teda-Daza and Zaghawa are Saharan branch members; Mande is the only well-defined sub-group within Niger-Congo (Susu-Yalunka, Soninke, Manding-Bambara-Dyula, Vai-Kono, Khasonke etc.), the Mande-tan/Mande-fu division from Delafosse is invalid; Hausa is Chadic (Afro-Asiatic).

Kwa languages include Yoruba, Igala, Nupe, Edo, Idoma, Igbo, Akan-Guang, Ewe-Fon, Ga-Adangme and the Togo Remnant languages; Greenberg doubts whether Kru and Ijo belong; Benue-Congo includes Plateau, Jukunoid, Cross River (Efik-Ibibio) and Bantoid including Bantu and Tiv.

Southern Cushitic and Eastern Cushitic in East Africa; Nilotic divided into Western (Luo, Dinka-Nuer), Eastern (Bari, Karamojong, Teso, Turkana, Masai) and Southern (Nandi, Suk, Tatoga); Meinhof's Hamitic Masai versus Greenberg's Nilotic.

Africa is geographically massive: about 30 million square km, 8000 km north to south and 5700 km east to west, smooth coast, average altitude 660 m, Rift valleys 4000 km from the Red Sea to Mozambique with lakes (Nyasa, Tanganyika, Kivu, Edward, Albert, Victoria, Turkana); the author rejects geographical determinism, saying geography impeded or promoted but did not determine human activity, and that coastal inhospitability and isolation are exaggerated (the Atlantic was not used before the 15th century because sail could not beat the trade winds).

Climate zones: equatorial (over 2000 mm), tropical sub-zones (1500-2000 mm, 600-1500 mm, under 600 mm in the Sahel), desert (under 250 mm, Sahara under 100 mm), Mediterranean at the two tips; mechanisms: intertropical front, harmattan, Guinean monsoon, cold Canaries and Benguela currents explain the coastal deserts of Mauritania and Namibia.

The Sahara, nearly a third of the continent over some 15 degrees of latitude, was humid in the past and never an absolute barrier: crossed by caravan routes for centuries, but a filter limiting Mediterranean influence in agriculture, architecture and crafts and isolating much of Africa.

Niger: flows in a large loop from the Atlantic fringe towards the Sahara then to the Gulf of Guinea, interior delta of Macina near Timbuktu, two floods (upper and lower) in the rainy season; Nile 6700 km, average flow under 3000 cubic metres per second with six cataracts below Khartoum; Zaire discharges about 40 000 cubic metres per second with 32 rapids between Stanley Pool and the estuary; rivers are poor channels but encouraged contact.

Brown structured soils north of the Sudanese tropical ferruginous belt, with contrasting seasons under herbaceous cover, were of great agricultural value and permitted agrarian cultures associated with the great Sudanese empires, though sensitive to gullying; tropical ferruginous and bowe laterite soils are unstable and of limited farming value.

Conclusion on resources: Nubian and Kushite gold exploited by ancient Egypt; Sudanese and Zimbabwe gold supported North Africa and Near East and the black empires; iron traded between forest and tropics in ancient times; Saharan salt mines linked the black Sudan states and the Arabo-Berber north; zonal complementarity underlay long-standing trade.

Indian Ocean monsoons let Arab and Indian ships sail to Africa and back; contacts were confined to the coast because Asian seafarers wished to trade rather than colonise; the Mozambique and Agulhas currents bring humidity to the south-east; the Rift valleys and lakes played a remarkable role in movement and settlement of peoples.

Southern highlands above 1500 m bounded by the Great Escarpment up to 3000 m; the Zambezi falls 110 m at Victoria Falls before Kariba gorge; soils under dry forest in the Zambezi countries were lightly gullied; Kalahari desert is more open to oceanic influence than the Sahara since the continent is narrower.

Downstream from Khartoum the Nile passes six rapids (the Cataracts) before the Mediterranean; with 6700 km it is the longest African river but not powerful; from Antiquity it has been one of the world's most useful rivers.

Minerals and early technology: lithic materials (obsidian from the Rift, flint and chert, quartzite for Acheulian tools, chalcedony), pigments (haematite, manganese, kaolin) and mud; iron ore (ferruginous laterite or ferricrete) is widespread in the grassland savanna so ironworking spread quickly, whereas copper and tin were localised and Africa had no widespread bronze culture, apart from copper users in north-east Ethiopia and the Luba of Shaba and a copper age in Mauritania five centuries before our era.

Vegetal resources: grassland over 50 per cent of Africa, desert about 30, forest under 20; savanna seed-agriculture complex domesticated between the fourth and second millennium before our era and the forest vegeculture complex (yam, oil palm); fire used regularly by about 60 000 years ago, creating derived savanna as far south as 6 degrees north in West Africa; Mabogunje says Africa's contribution to domestication has been modest compared with Asia and relies on Vavilov, a view the volume's chapter 27 revises.

Grassland easy to traverse favoured large movements and the emergence of states; Mabogunje suggests states in the grassland dispersed weaker groups into mountains, arid wastes or forest; African population to 1650 put at 100 million, over 20 per cent of the world (Carr-Saunders), now about 10 per cent, with the savanna holding most people until slave raiding and colonisation.

Animal and soil resources: domesticated animals limited to ass, cat, guinea fowl, sheep and cow; first Neolithic pastoralists in the Sahara in the fifth millennium before our era or earlier, driven out by drying after about 2500 before our era (Clark); tsetse belt between 14 degrees north and south restricted large livestock, draught animals and the wheel, while riding animals encouraged mounted aggression and state domination of sedentary peoples; malarial mosquito and sickle-cell trait; locust invasions of 1847-54, 1892-1910, 1930-44 in Central Africa; soils: really fertile soils are scattered, such as East African volcanic loams and Nile alluvium; lateritic crusts limit northern West Africa and the Zaire margins.

Conclusion says nature was unusually kind and that easy existence led communities to side-step the 'agonizing demands of social evolution', so that far-sighted leaders' impact was not cumulative, and slave raiding was possible because of a failure to build cohesive organisations; this environmental-moral reading contradicts the same chapter's early statement that nature is only permissive and conflicts with Diarra (ch. 13) and the course's insistence on endogenous dynamism.

Fertile conditions of the Nile valley (rich alluvium and social management) were later reproduced in a few areas such as the Bend of the Niger at the emergence of the Ghana empire in the early medieval period.

Control of the gold trade between West and North Africa across the desert was one of the major reasons for the rise and fall of empires and kingdoms in the western Sudan in the medieval period (suggestion cited); gold and iron also attracted the Arabs to East Africa from the last millennium.

Cattle moved south through fly-free corridors; Mabogunje cites the migration of cattle owners some nine centuries ago who merged with others to form the Tutsi and Hutu society of present-day Rwanda and Burundi.

Africa's population is said to have been about 100 million by 1650, over 20 per cent of the world total, and the savanna zone's share fell with slave raiding from the sixteenth century; external slave raiding had a pernicious effect on development in the author's view.

Rapid spread of techniques and tools across grassland and the difficulty of finding the source region of innovations; large movements of people delineated by archaeology, ethnography, linguistics and history.

Interdisciplinary method: chronology often needs four sources (written, archaeology, linguistics, oral tradition); the master source varies by topic (none for prehistory or Pygmy societies) and is identified only after the research; sources are complementary: al-Bakri's Koumbi Saleh description is incomplete without excavation, and oral tradition led to the site; oral tradition should be collected before excavating and can narrow hypotheses; an eclipse map can decide between versions; drums, music and cowries (described by Ibn Battuta in 1352 at Mali's court) are historical sources.

Linguistics solved the Lobi circular ruins: a Portuguese origin suggested from de Barros was ruled out by the road line and fresh plaster coating; the Wiili and Birifor name kol na wo ('stables for foreigners' cows') and Koulango pottery style, with migration traditions, gave the date and builders; the Dagomba horsemen's language of the fourteenth century was lost to that of the Kusase women they married, so language contamination can work against the rulers.

Dynamic sociology: average reign length cannot be extrapolated backwards: Yatenga's brother-to-brother collateral succession gives different averages from Ouagadougou's father-to-son line, and Gan kings chosen among the youngest adults reigned longer; apparent stability may be bought at a human cost (Ethiopia and Ouagadougou eliminated or deported collaterals); statistics: a population of 10 000 differs from one of 10 million, so fourteenth-century armies must not be pictured on twentieth-century scale.

Method: loose cooperation is inadequate, grafted interdisciplinary teams with joint questions are better; unitary societies need integrated histories (Konkomba study by Tait and Fage); Asian rice was domesticated where an African strain already existed and manioc where the yam grew; Mande expansion was the result of technology, trade, language, politics and religion; Mali had no metalled roads or bureaucracy, rulers opted for decentralisation, and most life went on in independent villages; iron guinze coins of Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia served as coin, protector of land and spirit resting-place.

Barter of salt for gold across the Sahara (later slaves for guns) may well have been the main factor behind the rise of West African kingdoms and empires; disparity in armament was probably decisive in letting early Ghana kings (like the Assyrians in Egypt and Shaka) establish hegemony; Ibn Battuta's episode on the Bure people shows the Mali emperor, failing to assimilate them, recognised their cultural independence; cowries at the Mali court were used as coinage, adornment and ceremonial items.

Zimbabwe: its structures above and below ground make sense only through gold mines and their defence plus religion; disparity in armament helped Shaka establish hegemony; an excavation of Dyola, Senufo and Lobi initiation societies shows religion organised whole communities.

Benin artists: the same artists (Igbesanvan) carve wood and ivory while others work pottery and bronze; Asian rice and manioc were absorbed where African strains of rice and yam existed (internal forces modify outside influence).

Sahara prehistory: desert 5700 km east-west and 1500 km north-south, nearly 8.6 million square km; no sufficient stratigraphy anywhere and, apart from the Neolithic, no absolute dates, so chronology is relative; by about 1000 before our era it was already desert; research was long left to amateurs on trans-Saharan expeditions; 'European' labels (Chellean, Mousterian) imposed errors; Hugot says there was no Upper Palaeolithic or true Mesolithic in the Sahara, with the Aterian (possibly from about 35 000 before our era, ending 9000-7000) as terminal Palaeolithic, all hypothesis.

Saharan Neolithic is a technical explosion rather than a revolution, oldest sites fifth to sixth millennia before our era; five streams: Sudanese (from the Nile near Khartoum and Esh Shaheinab, with rich decorated pottery, fishing and hunting, no proof of farming), Guinean forest Neolithic (perhaps from Central Africa), Capsian-tradition Neolithic (Algerian plateaux, austere pottery, fine microliths, ostrich-egg beads), a coastal shell-midden Neolithic, and the Tenerean of Adrar Bous (green jasper, lotus-shaped points, Vaufrey saw Egyptian influence but Hugot finds none outside Tenere).

Cradle of agriculture claim: Hugot sets strict proof (pollen, traces of cultivated land, identifiable plant fossils), says tools such as hoes and grindstones are not proof, finds only wild berries (Celtis), Cucurbitaceae seeds, Ziziphus and wild grain on most sites; millet at Tichitt confirms Munson and Monod; stockraisers, not farmers, generally followed hunter-gatherers; the Neolithic ended as lakes shrank and people emigrated with herds; he doubts the Sahara was where north African cereals developed.

Dhar Tichitt (south-east Mauritania): dry-stone fortified villages, the only Saharan group meeting his definition of urbanism, beginning about 2000 before our era; millet grains in fossilised turf show millet eating from 1500 before our era; culture is African, possibly from Tilemsi to the east; Hugot says this works as a hypothesis only.

The Tassili stock-raisers were contemporaries of the 'flying gallop' chariot painters; Hugot suggests about the time the Sea Peoples attacked Egypt (a guess); cattle and dogs found at Aukar by 2000 before our era; Sudanese Neolithic people probably used reed boats called kaddei like those still in Chad; Atlantic coast shell mounds, some veritable tells, as far as Senegal.

Early Iron Age (about 400 before our era to 700 of our era): Shaw holds iron metallurgy was most unlikely to be independently invented in West Africa, which had no earlier metallurgy; Taruga iron-smelting sites carbon-dated fifth to third century before our era, Niger valley mounds show iron by the second century before our era; on present evidence knowledge of iron came not from Meroe but from the Carthaginian sphere in North Africa, perhaps via chariot-using Garamantes (chariot rock-engravings along the Fezzan-Niger bend route); iron-using nomad pressure may explain fortifying of Tichitt villages from the fifth or fourth century before our era (Akinjeir phase).

Nok: terracotta figurines found mostly in tin-mining gravels around the Jos plateau, bracketed by dates between 500 before our era and 200 of our era; Taruga carbon dates and one thermoluminescence date of 620 plus or minus 230 before our era; Nok finds cover an area about 480 km long; art historians see in them ancestry of Yoruba art 1000 years later and 640 km away; stone-age artefacts in the gravels are older admixture; at Taruga no stone-age material, so the Nok occupation site with a ground stone axe is rare.

Food production: wheat and barley are winter-rain crops that cannot easily be grown south of the intertropical front, so West African cereals needed domestication of local grasses: Sorghum bicolor by the first half of the second millennium before our era between the Sahara and the savanna from the Nile to Lake Chad, pearl millet, finger millet and African rice (probably middle Niger delta); at Tichitt around 1000 before our era pearl millet rose from 3 to 60 per cent of grain; yams in the moister zones perhaps domesticated 5000 years ago but without archaeological or botanical proof.

West Africa was hardly touched by a Bronze Age: a facies from Spain and Morocco reached Mauritania where nearly 130 copper objects were found and Akjoujt copper dates to the fifth century before our era; the Sahara link between Egypt and West Africa lapsed with the final desiccation in the third millennium before our era and was re-established only with the camel some 3000 years later; Shaw thinks attempts to link West African history with ancient Egypt for lustre are unnecessary.

West African Stone Age: no early hominid remains found but research is lacking, humid acid soils destroy bone; Tchadanthropus is fragmentary and uncertain (Homo habilis to erectus); Lake Chad was high from about 40 000 before our era, dry about 18 000 before our era with dunes at the latitude of Kano, and wetter from about 10 000; Kintampo culture with dwarf goats and cattle dated before 1400 before our era; Iwo Eleru microlithic levels with 9200 before our era near the base and pottery by about 3000 before our era; Sahel cattle herders at Karkarichinkat 2000-1500 before our era; Late Stone Age shell mounds in Ivory Coast from 1600 before our era to the fourteenth century of our era; sub-Saharan Early, Middle and Late Stone Age scheme endorsed by the Third Pan-African Congress.

Southward movement of Saharan cattle pastoralists in the third millennium before our era adopted local microlith technique; immigrants were probably proto-Nilo-Saharan speakers who adopted local Niger-Congo languages except large groups such as Songhay ancestors; Senegambian stone circles and lyre-shaped pillars with funerary dates in the seventh-eighth centuries of our era and a terminus post quem in the first century before our era; Tondidarou phalliform stones plundered.

By the end of the Early Iron Age the northern margin of West Africa had agriculture and iron technology and was ready for political development; Berbers with camels ferried gold north across the desert; the fame of 'Ghana, the land of gold' had reached Baghdad by the end of the eighth century (Levtzion); northern Sierra Leone shifted to iron only from the eighth century.

Nok art as ancestor of Yoruba forms is the view of some art historians (Fagg, Willett); southern Nigerian population density attributed to yam cultivation combined with oil-palm nuts; Fernando Po Late Stone Age with ground axes and a sixth-century date for its earliest stage, if correct; Afikpo assemblage 3000 to 1 before our era.

Herodotus's Carthaginian silent trade for West African gold is almost certainly based on fact, while Hanno's voyage account is probably a forgery (Picard, Mauny); contacts with the classical world were slender, sporadic and indirect; the Sahara link between Egypt and West Africa returned with the camel; iron-pointed spears replace the bow in rock-engravings of nomads.

Nile valley stone ages: Oldowan pebble tools confirmed in Egypt by 1971-74 excavations at Thebes (hominid tooth in early alluvial strata with choppers, Abbassia in 1925 earlier labelled eoliths); Acheulian with no break from Sudan to Egypt; Middle Stone Age groups (Nubian Mousterian about 45 000-33 000 before our era, Khormusian revised from 25 000-16 000 to 41 490-33 800 before our era); Aterian in the Libyan desert north-west of Abu Simbel in 1976; Late Stone Age and Mesolithic cultures proliferate (Jemaian, Sebilian, Hawarian, Qadian, Silsilian) but Debono warns names multiply from imperfect statistics.

Khartoumian, the earliest culture of the Neolithic Sudan (perhaps about 4000 before our era, uncertain): wattle huts, sophisticated pottery with wavy-line and dotted-line decoration, microlithic quartz tools, barbed bone harpoons, ostrich-eggshell beads, ritual tooth mutilation, dead buried in dwellings and described as a black race, the earliest in Africa; Shaheinabian derived from it, with smoothed red-slip pottery with black edging, gouges and polished bone axes, dwarf goat domesticated, features shared with the Fayum and early Predynastic and with Tibesti; Kadero burials about 3500-3000 before our era.

Nubia and Upper Egypt: Abkian about 3380-2985 before our era, black-edged pottery linking Nubian A-Group and Predynastic; Nubian A, B and C Groups kept prehistoric characteristics until the New Kingdom after contacts with Egypt slowed from the First Dynasty; southern Egypt (Tasian, Badarian with copper-encased quartz beads, Nagada I about 4000-3500, Nagada II about 3500-3100 before our era) and northern Egypt (Fayum, Merimde 4180-3580, Omarian A about 3300, Maadi with copper from Sinai) were two parallel cultural groups until unification, with the north ahead in urbanisation and the south in art.

Stone persisted in the Pharaonic age: flint knives at Abydos at peak quality under early dynasties; flint tools in Middle Kingdom Thebes no different from Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic types; half of 200 flint factories on the Thebes mound date from the New Kingdom; Debono writes that Tutankhamun is of the twenty-eighth dynasty and that Mirgissa lance points date from the twenty-eighth dynasty, which cannot be right (Tutankhamun belongs to the eighteenth dynasty and Mirgissa is a Middle Kingdom fortress); flint lance points copying metal ones at Mirgissa show metal was hard to obtain in remote Nubia.

Conclusion calls Neolithic a term with no precise meaning in Egypt, regrets lost Nubian archaeology under water, and warns that without stratigraphy there has been an undue tendency to coin new names from imperfect statistics and physico-chemical tests.

Ethnocentric 'Neolithic revolution' from the Near East is revised; Vavilov saw only the Abyssinian centre in Africa, Porteres added West African and East African centres; colonialist prejudice long played down African agriculture; Makalian wet phase (5500-2500 before our era) eased contacts and fishing settlement; gathering abundance on forest-savanna edges, East African plateaux and lake and river shores, around 9000 before our era, favoured domestication; Randles notes the most prestigious Bantu civilisations lie at savanna margins.

Cradles of African agriculture: Afro-Mediterranean (wheat, barley, olive), West African (sorghum, pearl millet, fonio, African rice, yams, oil palm, kola, Bambara groundnut), Nile-Abyssinian (teff, ensete, Arabian coffee, niger), Central African and East African (finger millet, sesame); three foci: Mediterranean, savanna-steppe cereals, forest horticulture (tubers, garden-orchard) with food-gathering; forest horticulture domesticated fewer plants than Asian or American wet forests; implements mostly hoe and digging stick, with an Egyptian-Ethiopian primitive plough; the savanna cereal centre is the most important; crucial domestication period 9000 to 5000 before our era, a guess awaiting archaeology.

Sorghum originated in Africa with several independent origins (wild S. arundinaceum for West African groups, S. verticilliflorum for east and south-east, S. aethiopicum for durra spread from Chad to India); African rice (Oryza glaberrima) recognised only about 1914, primary variation centre the central Niger delta and secondary centre Senegambia (upper Gambia and Casamance), spread to the Guinea coast; Asian rice (O. sativa) introduced possibly from the eighth century onward by Arabs on the East African coast or from the sixteenth by Europeans on the west; Strabo and Ibn Battuta (fourteenth century) mention rice in Africa.

Exchange with Asia: bananas, greater yam (Dioscorea alata), taro and possibly sugar cane arrived from tropical South-East Asia, perhaps via south-western Arabia and East Africa or early navigators landing in south-east Africa, and bananas helped agriculture gain a foothold in the forest; early migrants to Madagascar and the East African coast carried them; cattle, sheep and goats came via Egypt and the Nile valley though cattle ancestors Bos primigenius and B. brachyceros were hunted in Egypt; Wrigley: animal husbandry did not develop independently south of the Sahara; the authors conclude African agriculture was endogenous with outside additions.

The West African centre has two ranges: tropical (Senegambian, central Niger, Chad-Nilotic) with cereals, Coleus and shea butter, and sub-equatorial with yams (Dioscorea cayenensis, D. rotundata, D. dumetorum), oil palm, Telfairia and cola; rice-growing methods include mangrove swamp rice fields in Senegal and Guinea using spades (Serer, Dyula Bayot, Baga).

South-East Asian plants (banana, taro, greater yam, possibly sugar cane) arrived on African shores perhaps through south-western Arabia and East Africa; migrants to Madagascar and the east coast carried domesticates; the East African and Bantu centre includes finger millet and sesame; this supports the Indian Ocean dimension of the origins debate.
Abyssinian centre: affinities with the Near East (wheats, barleys, legumes) and its own Arabian coffee, ensete (Abyssinian banana), teff and niger; plants from Asia passed into Africa through it.

The Nile valley is a north-south and east-west channel of communication (6500 km, cataract difficulties exaggerated); Saharo-Sudanese Neolithic is earlier than Egyptian (Amekni about 6700 before our era versus Jericho proto-Neolithic 6800; pottery in Nubia 5750 before our era, in the Fayum about 4400), so the Nile Neolithic may descend from the African Neolithic, although the Asiatic origin remains an unproved hypothesis because the Delta sites are unexplored; Fayum A 4400, Merimde 4100, El Omari 3300 before our era.

Social systems in the lower Nile: controlled irrigation perhaps began in Nagada II (about 3070 before our era plus or minus 290) and drove the first social organisation, ethnic groups around provincial centres joining into northern and southern confederations; the Nile flood is variable (only ten of thirty floods from 1871 to 1900 satisfactory; floods under Osorkon III in 754 and Taharqa in 683 before our era); copper appears before gold in Egypt, maybe by independent discovery, with faience discovered together; no break between Neolithic and Predynastic, so Vercoutter prefers the term Predynastic.

Predynastic phases: Early (Badarian, Fayum A), Ancient (Amratian, about 3800), Middle (Gerzean) and Late (about three generations); Seth of Ombos versus Horus of Behdet, northern victory, then southern kings from Hierakonpolis and This forming the Thinite dynasties; Vercoutter notes unification dates are about 3000 or as late as 2800 before our era and that the texts are projected back onto archaeology; Pat, Rekhyt and Henemmet as old human groupings.

Upper Nile: Shaheinab and Early Khartoum, Abkian fishermen with stone fish-traps at the Second Cataract giving rise to Nubian A-Group (about 3800-2200 before our era; Early 3800-3200, Classical 3200-2800, Late 2800-2200); Group A farmers built dams at low water; Classical A had a population explosion and imports of Gerzean vases for ivory and ebony, vanished about 2800 before our era probably from raids by First Dynasty pharaohs; copper ore deposits in Nubia suggest local copper needles.

Egypt's society was flexible, not rigid castes (Herodotus and Strabo wrong); estates of family, temple and king; Amun's estate under the eighteenth dynasty is given as 81 322 men, 421 362 cattle, 433 gardens, 2393 square km of fields, 83 boats and 65 villages (from Breasted); strike at Deir el-Medina in 1165 before our era; a professional army after the Hyksos, becoming a military caste; the upper Nile depopulated after Egyptian occupation from 1580 before our era; a Sudanese kingdom of Napata from about 750 before our era stretching from the confluence of the Niles to the Second Cataract and later the Mediterranean, with Lower Nubia 750-650, with matriarchy important in the ruling family.

Metals: gold in Nubia between the First and Third Cataracts (name Nubia perhaps from noub); bronze appeared about 2000 before our era, widespread by 1500, never replaced copper; Kerma had 130 copper daggers from about 1800-1700 before our era, more than all Egypt, unanalysed so copper versus bronze unknown; meteoric iron only until the end of the eighth century before our era, smelted iron spreading in the lower valley then and as common as bronze and copper a century later; iron may have been worked earlier in the upper valley (hence more under the Twenty-fifth Dynasty) but did not become widespread until the first century before our era with Meroitic civilisation.

Meroe's role in disseminating iron in Africa is not as obvious as used to be thought (Shinnie, Trigger); iron may have come from North Africa via Saharan caravan routes (Huard); this joins Shaw's chapter 24 argument that West African iron did not come from Meroe.

Conclusion: Africa as a principal centre of human emergence (Australopithecus, Homo habilis); adaptation by morphology and environment; Ki-Zerbo cites speculative claims (aquatic ape theory of Morgan; negroid Aurignacian statuettes per Furon; a Negro race covering the world 30 000 years ago in Science et Avenir 1954) that sit beside firmer evidence; prehistory continued in some regions until about the year 1000 and in some groups to the 19th century apart from metal tools.

Mode of production: Ki-Zerbo says African societies had no private ownership of land, no feudalism and no slavery as understood in the West (citing Suret-Canale, Chesneaux, Maquet), that slavery was marginal and captives were integrated, with massive slavery in Dahomey, Asante and Zanzibar a product of external capitalism, that productive forces stagnated for at least 500 years, and that colonial rule created the periphery; these claims are contested by the supplied books (Lovejoy, Manning, Rodney on slavery and land) and by his own earlier chapters.

Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) is presented as founder of history as a science with asabiyya cycles and the claim that customs depend on how a people secures subsistence; Marx's 'Asiatic mode of production' is judged not to fit African structures; stateless villages and decentralised empires such as Mali (Ibn Battuta) meant distance mitigated the capitals' sway and subjects could flee.

Production surplus was modest save where state monopolies of gold, ivory or salt existed (Ghana, Asante); redistribution at festivals explains Mansa Musa's lavishness at his pilgrimage in 1324; Maquet: except for redistribution there was no economic counterpart for the surpluses rulers extracted.

Captives in Kayor could be commanders-in-chief; in Asante it was forbidden to allude to anyone's servile origin so a former captive could become a village chief; massive slavery in Dahomey and Asante in the 18th and 19th centuries stemmed from external economic influence in Ki-Zerbo's view; nobility did not trade; Mossi teng-soba 'master of the land' retained the land after conquest.

Exploitation of Africa peaked three times: in antiquity (Nile valley and Roman provinces as Rome's granary and source of wild animals, slaves, gladiators), from the sixteenth century in the slave trade, and in the nineteenth century in colonisation; Ki-Zerbo says capital accumulation and industrial revolution in Europe needed enforced contributions from Africa, Asia and the Americas.

Rome treated the Nile valley and North African provinces as its granary and drew wild animals, slaves and gladiators from Africa; African trade barriers remained a factor in the Nile and Niger valleys.

St Augustine (354-430) and Ibn Khaldun are named as African thinkers of history: Augustine broke with cyclic time, Ibn Khaldun made history a science resting on verified evidence; both are used to show Africa's own philosophies of history.

South of the equator and in most of East Africa there was no Neolithic because food production spread only with the Iron Age (which began in most regions about 2000 years ago); in the highlands of Kenya and northern Tanzania herding, with perhaps a little agriculture, appears in the terminal Late Stone Age 2000 to 3000 years ago, with pottery and stone bowls; at Narosura (southern Kenya) 95 per cent of identified fauna are domestic, 57 per cent sheep and goats and 39 per cent cattle, killed young for goats and old for cattle, so cattle kept for milk and perhaps blood; Neolithization may have reached the Ethiopian highlands and been carried south by small-scale movements of Cushitic-speaking peoples.

In the first few centuries of our era Late Stone Age hunter-gatherers of southern Africa were replaced over much of the subcontinent by agricultural peoples with metallurgy, most likely an advance guard of Bantu-speaking groups from a homeland thought to lie in the north-west (Chad and Cameroon); there was no Neolithic stage, and no cultivation before the Early Iron Age; some south-western Late Stone Age groups had sheep by the first century before our era and later cattle, nomadic pastoralists identified with the Khoi-Khoi whose pastoral phase can hardly have begun before about 300 before our era and ended in the eighteenth century of our era; no pastoral occupation site had been excavated, and the source of the stock (Sudanic speakers or Early Iron Age migrants) is debated; earliest dated rock paintings from the Apollo 11 shelter in Namibia are 28 000 b.p. while much rock art may be only 2000 to 3000 years old.
